subject: chemistry
title: Pure Elements
welcome_lead: Meet the building blocks: substances made of only one type of atom.
meta_desc: Discover what elements are and how they appear on the periodic table in this KS3 chemistry adventure.
final_note: You now know that elements are the purest form of matter.

concepts.def: A substance made of only one type of atom.
The tiny building block of all matter.

walkthroughs.body_html:
An element is a substance made of only one type of atom. You cannot break an element down into anything simpler using chemistry.

One element = one type of atom.

Every element has a chemical symbol. Examples: H (hydrogen), O (oxygen), Fe (iron), Na (sodium), Au (gold).

The first letter is always a capital, the second is always lowercase.

Copper wires, gold jewellery, helium balloons, the oxygen in your lungs and the carbon in pencil lead are all elements.

There are about 118 known elements organised on the periodic table.

mcqs.q: Why do tertiary halogenoalkanes typically react via SN1 rather than SN2?
options: The tertiary carbocation intermediate is stabilised by three alkyl groups (positive inductive effect), making the SN1 pathway favourable.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN1 because they are more reactive in every way.
Kp uses the volumes of each gas in the mixture.

mcqs.q: In a standard hydrogen electrode used as a reference, what is the assigned electrode potential?
options: The standard hydrogen electrode actually has zero potential because hydrogen has no charge.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.
Exactly 0 V by convention — all other electrode potentials are measured relative to it.

mcqs.q: What does Kp use instead of concentrations?
options: Partial pressures of each gaseous component at equilibrium.
The standard hydrogen electrode has a potential of -1 V to balance copper at +1 V.
Kp uses the total pressure of the system raised to the stoichiometric coefficients.
Kp uses the volumes of each gas in the mixture.
